metadata.title: Light Shaders
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: Take over what a light does to every pixel

beats.narration_text: Light Shaders. Learn what the light function does and what Godot hands it, then use it to build a sweeping lighthouse beam and a ring that spreads from a lamp.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Lighting in a two-D game feels built in: you place a light, and Godot does the rest. Most people think that is where your control ends. It is not. A shader can replace it.

show.event: backspaces 'You can't touch it' and types 'A shader can replace it'

props.text:
Lighting is built in.
You can't touch it.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A pixel is one dot of the picture. A texture is an image a shader can read. The canvas is the surface two-D things are drawn on. A vector is a bundle of two to four numbers. And a mask is a number from zero to one, for each pixel, saying how much of something to show.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
one dot of the picture on screen
an image a shader can read by address
the surface that 2D things are drawn on
a bundle of two to four numbers
a number from 0 to 1 per pixel saying how much of something to show

beats.narration_text: In a two-D game, a light is a soft glow. Same scene, same light, and one function later, that glow is a beam sweeping the ground. The function is called light, and before this film ends, you will have written it.

Caption: 'light(): runs once per pixel for each light that touches it'.

beats.narration_text: Godot has two kinds of two-D light. A point light shines out from one spot, like a lamp. A directional light shines the same way everywhere, like the sun. This film works mostly with the lamp.

shot.visual_intent: Two panels on the cream stage, each a short strip of six outlined floor tiles. Left: a pale lamp disc above the strip with rays fanning out to every tile, label 'point light'. Right: a sun disc far up with parallel rays slanting the same way onto the strip, label 'directional light'. Grey captions under them: 'like a lamp', 'like the sun'.

beats.narration_text: A light needs a dim scene to show against. A two-D scene starts fully lit, so a light can only brighten what is already bright. Add a Canvas Modulate node, which tints everything, and set it dim. That tint is the ambient light.

shot.visual_intent: A real Godot render in a framed window: a cream-tiled floor already fully lit, a lamp that barely shows. At 'set it dim' the tint eases in, the floor goes dusk blue and the lamp's glow blooms. Caption: 'ambient light: the tint where no lamp reaches'; a label 'Canvas Modulate' lands as the node is named.

beats.narration_text: A soft glow is a texture. Godot's docs give the recipe. Give the light a gradient texture, set its fill to radial, and run the gradient from opaque white to transparent white. The transparent part becomes the soft edge.

beats.narration_text: A point light has a few settings. Its texture sets its shape. Its scale sets how far it reaches. Color tints it, and energy is how strong it is. Change each one, and the same lamp lights the same ground differently.

shot.visual_intent: A real Godot render: one lamp on the dusk floor. Its glow first grows (scale), then shifts from warm to cool (color), then dims and brightens (energy); a small label names each setting as the voice says it. Caption: 'reach: how far the light spreads · energy: how strong it is'.

lecture.why: Each setting changes the glow differently, and a real render shows all three effects on the same lamp.

beats.narration_text: Lights add. Two lamps overlapping make the overlap brighter, and three make it brighter still. Underneath, the dim ambient stays put, whether a light reaches a pixel or not.

beats.narration_text: Godot's rule, measured. The pixel is the surface color times the total of the ambient and every light. A grey surface of one half, an ambient of point two, two lamps of point four each: the pixel reads one half.

shot.visual_intent: The rule as outlined swatch boxes on the cream stage: [surface 0.5] x ( [ambient 0.2] + [lamp 0.4] + [lamp 0.4] ) = [pixel 0.5], each swatch filled with the grey of its own number. Small grey credit: 'measured · Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · 0, 1, 2, 3 lamps: 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7'.
shot.motion_claim: The two lamp boxes slide in one after the other and the result swatch fills to the sum, ending on one half.

beats.narration_text: A two-D shader can have three functions. Vertex places corners, and fragment colors each pixel. The third, light, runs for every pixel and every light that reaches it, and asks: how much does this lamp add here?

shot.visual_intent: A header strip of three outlined boxes, 'vertex()  corners', 'fragment()  pixels', 'light()  lamps'; the third is ringed. Below, one pixel cell on a small floor strip with two lamp dots; an arrow runs from each lamp to the pixel and a small 'light()' box answers each arrow with its own swatch, the swatches piling up. Caption: 'light(): once per pixel, for each light that touches it'.

shot.motion_claim: The two arrows travel from the lamps to the pixel; each is answered by a swatch and the swatches pile up.

beats.narration_text: Add a function called light to a shader, and it replaces Godot's default lighting for that sprite. Even an empty one. The lamp still lights the blob, but the ground ignores it. The function belongs to the sprite, not to the lamp.

Code card at left with the empty light() function and a definition tag on its first line ('light(): runs once per pixel for each light that touches it'); at right a real Godot window: the lit floor and the blob. At 'Even an empty one' the glow leaves the floor (only the dusk look is left) while the blob stays lit. A ring settles on the blob, labels 'default lighting' (blob) and 'empty light()' (ground).

beats.narration_text: The smallest light function returns one flat answer: point two grey. Add a lamp, and this card brightens by point two. Add another, and it brightens again. Light runs once for each lamp, and Godot adds the answers.

beats.narration_text: Inside light, Godot hands you built-ins, values written in capital letters. Color is this pixel's own color, and U V is its address. Light color and light energy describe the lamp. You hand back one value, also called light: what this lamp adds.

shot.visual_intent: A box labelled light(). Four arrows come in from the left, labelled in monospace capitals COLOR, UV, LIGHT_COLOR, LIGHT_ENERGY; one arrow leaves to the right labelled LIGHT. Caption: 'built-in: a value the engine hands to a function, or collects from it'. A grey note: 'more in the docs: NORMAL, SCREEN_UV ...'.
shot.motion_claim: The four inputs slide into the box one after another and the single answer leaves on the right.

lecture.why: The idea is values in and one value out; a box with arrows is exactly that, while the docs table has more rows than the voice can name.

beats.narration_text: Light runs last. Fragment runs first and sets the pixel's color, which arrives in light as the built-in color. Then light runs once for each lamp, and Godot adds all the answers to the dim ambient look. That sum is the pixel.

shot.visual_intent: A strip left to right on the cream stage: 'fragment()  sets color' -> 'light()  once per lamp' (two small lamp dots feed it, each answer a small swatch) -> '+ dim ambient look' -> a pixel swatch. A token travels the strip; the arrows are drawn shapes pointing only forward.
shot.motion_claim: A token passes fragment, splits into one pass per lamp, and the answers join the ambient look to make the pixel.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: An order of work is a token moving forward through stages, never back.

beats.narration_text: Rebuild Godot's default. The color is the surface, times the lamp's color, times its energy. The fourth number, alpha, passes straight through. Rendered both ways, the same scene differs in no pixel at all.

The alpha line carries the tag 'alpha: how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid' as alpha is spoken.

beats.narration_text: Or let time shape it. Multiply the light by the absolute value of a sine of time, and the lamp breathes. No animation player and no game code: the shader does it every frame.

beats.act: III · Which Way Is the Light?
beats.narration_text: Now, direction. Light direction is a vector, an arrow from this pixel toward the lamp, always length one. A pixel left of the lamp gets an arrow pointing right. A pixel above it gets an arrow pointing down.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Which Way Is the Light?' (serif 40) top-left. A lamp dot in the middle of a pixel-grid field; eight pixel dots on a ring around it; from each pixel dot a short arrow of the same length points at the lamp. Labels 'LIGHT_DIRECTION' and 'length 1'. The dot left of the lamp has its arrow pointing right, the dot above has its arrow pointing down, each ringed in turn. Caption: 'vector: a bundle of two to four numbers'.
shot.motion_claim: An arrow sprouts from every pixel dot and every one of them aims at the lamp.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: Arrows from many pixels converging on one lamp is the definition itself; the colour wheel would hide which way they point.

beats.act: III · Which Way Is the Light?
beats.narration_text: To see a number, use it as brightness. Take the arrow's x number, from minus one to one, and squeeze it into zero to one. Multiply the lamp by it. Left of the lamp, full strength. Right of the lamp, nothing.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the across line, the rgb line that multiplies by it); at right a real Godot window: the smooth glow becomes a lamp that is strongest on its left and fades to nothing on its right. Labels 'full' (left of the lamp) and 'none' (right of it).

beats.act: III · Which Way Is the Light?
beats.narration_text: Turn that number into a mask with step. Step gives zero below an edge, and one at or above it. Use an edge of zero, multiply the light by the result, and only the left half of the lamp stays on.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (mask = step(0.0, LIGHT_DIRECTION.x), the rgb line, LIGHT); at right a real Godot window: the smooth left-to-right fade snaps into a sharp half lamp, the left half on and the right half dark, with a clean vertical edge through the lamp. The mask line carries the tag 'step(edge, x): 0 below the edge, 1 from the edge up'.

beats.narration_text: So when does a job belong in light? When it depends on a lamp: its direction, its distance, its color. A pattern on the surface alone belongs in fragment, and a wobble in the corners in vertex. Ask where the effect comes from.

the surface alone: a pattern, a gradient
the shape's corners: a lean, a wobble
props.note: A rule of thumb from this film's runs · Godot 4.7 shader reference

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A pixel is its surface times the total of the ambient and every light. Writing light replaces the default, and you can rebuild it exactly. Light direction is an arrow from the pixel toward the lamp. Aim an arrow, compare it with a dot, and a mask becomes a beam. Light position and light vertex give a distance, and distance makes rings. Those positions are window pixels, so they ignore your camera zoom.

Writing light replaces the default, and you can rebuild it exactly.
Light direction is an arrow from the pixel toward the lamp.
Aim an arrow, compare it with a dot, and a mask becomes a beam.
Light position and light vertex give a distance, and distance makes rings.
Those positions are window pixels, so they ignore your camera zoom.
